race_context: The 'Frankfort Community School Board' seats belong to Community Schools of Frankfort, the public school district for Frankfort, the Clinton County seat {csf_home}{sboe_csf_plan}. Its seven residence districts cover the city's five wards, Center Township outside the city and Union Township {sboe_csf_plan}. Federal data list five schools and 2,972 students in 2024-25 {nces_csf}. Dr. Matthew (Matt) Rhoda has been superintendent since July 1, 2022, after serving as assistant superintendent {csf_home}{ft_rhoda_named}.

The Board of School Trustees has seven members, one living in each of seven districts, but every voter in the school corporation votes for every seat on the ballot; members serve four-year terms, Districts 1-3 are elected in 2024, 2028 and so on, and Districts 4-7 in 2022, 2026 and so on {sboe_csf_plan}. So each 2026 race elects one member, matching the state list's 'vote for 1' {sboe_csf_plan}{in_list}. Current members are Sandra Miller (president), Robert Marcum (vice president), James McQuade (secretary), Kristen Beardsley, Mandi Mitchell, Joel Tatum and Mark Sanders {csf_board}.

Who holds the seats now: all four were filled without opposition in 2022, when Kristen Beardsley won District 4, Amanda 'Mandi' Mitchell District 5, Joel Tatum District 6 and Sandra Miller District 7 {ft_2022_results}. Beardsley is not on the 2026 ballot, so District 4 will have a new member {ft_2022_results}{in_list}. Mitchell (District 5) and Tatum (District 6) are unopposed, and Miller faces two challengers in District 7 {in_list}.

Party labels: 2026 is the first year Indiana school board candidates could list a party {ft_party_split}. The state list shows Edward H Niehaus and Sandra Miller as Republicans, Jennifer Fitch as a Democrat, and the other candidates as Nonpartisan {in_list}. Candidates filed by petition with at least 10 voter signatures; filing closed at noon June 18, 2026, and there was no school board primary {ccdn_filing_2026}.

Staffing and enrollment (2026): Superintendent Rhoda announced a reduction of 16 teaching positions for 2026-27, saying in a March 2026 video that the cuts align staffing with enrollment, which has declined over the past decade {ft_staff_video}. At a February 2026 board meeting, Brenda Buckingham-Ehrmann, speaking for the Frankfort Education Association, urged the board to reconsider the reductions {ft_fea_cuts}.

Budget and property taxes: this guide found no reporting on how the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) affects the district's budget, and no operating or safety referendum. The board's 2026-27 meetings are scheduled for Oct. 20, Nov. 17 and Dec. 15, 2026 {csf_board}.

Facilities: a renovation of Frankfort Middle School, described in June 2025 as a $25 million project begun in 2024, added a secure main entrance, relocated front office, and a performing arts center with more than 600 seats {ft_fms_reno}. In August 2026 the board heard updates on ongoing construction at both Frankfort High School and Frankfort Middle School {ft_gem_city}.

Policies and safety: at a July 29, 2025 special meeting the board revised its attendance policy to match new state law aimed at chronic absenteeism (parent notes for illness no longer count as excused absences) and updated its bullying policy {ft_policy_2025}. Frankfort police officers serve as school resource officers under a 2022 agreement with the city {ft_sro_2022}.

Academics: the board recognized Frankfort High School's Gem City University early college program in August 2026 after it won a Change-Maker Award at the Early College Summit {ft_gem_city}. This guide did not check the district's state accountability grades.

Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum, questionnaire or news coverage of the candidates' views. The Clinton County Democratic Party announced a public meet-and-greet for Oct. 13, 2026; the announcement does not name which candidates will attend {ccdn_dem_meet}.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, unopposed; appointed to the board in 2019 and elected to the District 5 seat without opposition in 2022 {ccdn_mitchell_2019}{ft_2022_results}{in_list}.
background: Known as Mandi Mitchell; a Frankfort native and Frankfort graduate {ccdn_mitchell_2019}{ft_2022_results}.

When appointed in May 2019 she was treasurer of the Clinton Prairie School Corporation; then-superintendent Don DeWeese said the board believed she could bring 'some expertise on school funding' {ccdn_mitchell_2019}.
path_to_ballot: Sworn in in May 2019 to replace Jeff Tatum, who had resigned {ccdn_mitchell_2019}. Elected to District 5 unopposed in 2022 with 1,901 votes {ft_2022_results}.
Filed for reelection without a party label; the state lists her as Nonpartisan and as the only candidate {in_list}.
on_incumbent: Is a current board member. In 2019 she said she wanted to serve on a board that prepares students to pursue whatever goals they choose {ccdn_mitchell_2019}. No 2026 statement on the board's record was found.

review_flags.summary: On Oct. 11, 2017, Frankfort Mayor Chris McBarnes and Clerk-Treasurer Judy Sheets announced that Parks Superintendent Joel Tatum was terminated after he declined a different position in the department, following city review of 'financial variances' in Parks Department operations; they said the State Board of Accounts might be involved and made no further comment {ccdn_tatum_2017}. A Feb. 21, 2018 statement issued by Jeff Tatum on his behalf said the prosecutor found no basis for charges and that the State Board of Accounts found no missing money or misappropriation, while acknowledging that record-keeping and deposits could have been better {ccdn_tatum_stmt}. No charges were reported.
review_flags.note: The 2017-18 articles do not mention the school board; the tie to the candidate rests on the same name and the same job (the Joel Tatum hired as parks superintendent in 2023 was identified as a CSF board member). The State Board of Accounts findings come only from Tatum's own statement and were not independently checked.

review_flags.summary: The City of Frankfort announced on Jan. 21, 2025 that Parks Superintendent Joel Tatum had resigned effective immediately, after reports of USDA violations filed in December 2024 and the deaths of animals at the TPA Park Aviary and Petting Zoo {ccdn_tatum_resign}{ft_tatum_resign}. Mayor Judy Sheets thanked him 'for his dedication to our parks' {ft_tatum_resign}. Tatum was identified as a sitting CSF board member when he took the job in 2023 {ft_tatum_sworn}. No response from Tatum was found.
review_flags.note: The articles do not state that he was asked to resign or found responsible; USDA findings were not reviewed.
